source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for NL claim sets (QXR): experimental setting
finding: QXR was tested with one oracle call per query, no majority voting, no repeated queries. The paper says repeated-query independence is used only in the theory.
numbers: r = 1 call per query; scope set C = {F} (whole set); temperature 0.0 on Bedrock; 7 judges: Sonnet 3.7, Sonnet 4, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.6, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-OSS-120B, Mistral Large 2407.
quote: We do not use majority voting or repeated querying in the empirical evaluation
limits: QXR was never run against a noisy or non-monotone oracle with repeats. Gap 3 stays open.
agent_relevance: Any claim that the localise-then-delete loop is robust to a noisy judge is untested.

source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for NL claim sets (QXR): limitations section
finding: The authors state that real LLM judgments may be noisy, prompt-sensitive or non-monotonic, and that their guarantees assume monotone, perfect judging. Weighted repair and a graded (probability) oracle are listed as extensions, not tested.
numbers: Graded oracle idea: oracle returns p_incons(S) in [0,1], threshold, abstain or re-query near boundary. Weighted repair: per-claim deletion cost, minimum-cost hitting set. No numbers reported for either.
quote: real LLM judgments may be noisy, prompt-sensitive, or non-monotonic
limits: Both fixes are sketches in the discussion. Experiments use claim sets of N=30 (RAMDocs) and moderate sizes, no code or reasoning chains.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: weighted hitting set is proposed, not shown to fix noise. Needs our own test: flip oracle answers at rate e and measure recall.

source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for NL claim sets (QXR): prompt-sensitivity table (appendix F, Table 5), VitaminC subset
finding: Alternative direct-judge prompts (chain-of-thought, decomposition, few-shot, self-consistency prompt) all keep high precision but low recall. QXR beats the original direct baseline in recall for all 5 judges. This is a prompt-style comparison, not an equal-token comparison.
numbers: Recall, direct zero-shot vs self-consistency prompt vs QXR: Claude-3.7 .681/.547/.975; Claude-4 .928/.768/.983; DeepSeek-R1 .860/.718/.990; GPT-OSS-120B .876/.475/.995; Mistral Large 2 .568/.522/.978. QXR F1: .965/.960/.981/.975/.972. Original direct F1: .912/.915/.837/.953/.739.
limits: Self-consistency prompt lowered recall below zero-shot in all 5 models. Number of samples and total tokens not equalised; alternative prompts were run on a dataset subset.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partly answered: re-asking the all-at-once judgement did not fix over-pruning. Cost parity with QXR (many more calls) is still not measured.

source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for NL claim sets (QXR): cost statements
finding: No measured call or token counts are reported for QXR. The paper only gives a bound: uncached token cost is at most O(Q) times a single full-set judgment, with Q = O(I*m*k*log N); localisation queries usually hold fewer claims.
numbers: Pairwise baseline would need N(N-1)/2 = 435 (N=30) or 4,950 (N=100) calls; these are the baseline's counts, not QXR's.
quote: QXR 's token cost is at most O(Q) times that of a single full-set judgment
limits: Without measured calls, nobody can say whether QXR wins at equal tokens against best-of-N. Authors say approximate localisation may be preferable when budget is limited.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 open: we must log calls and tokens ourselves.

source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for NL claim sets (QXR): benchmark task shape
finding: All three benchmarks are claim sets: VitaminC, FEVER and RAMDocs. Claims come from Wikipedia revisions or chunked retrieved snippets. No code, no reasoning chain, no circuit or software diagnosis.
numbers: RAMDocs: N = 30 claims, |U_gold| = 10 gold conflicts. VitaminC Sonnet 4.5 recall .617 to .957; Opus 4.6 .574 to .968. FEVER gains smaller; direct judging already strong for some models.
quote: preservation-oriented alternative when retaining unaffected information justifies additional oracle calls
limits: Authors say structured repair need not be preferable when direct judging is already reliable. No tests on faulty code or reasoning chains.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 open for QXR itself. Nearest evidence is from different methods (see d06, d07).

source: Zheng et al. (2025) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Locating the earliest wrong step in a reasoning chain is hard for LLMs and much harder on harder problems. Prompted critic models beat most process reward models. The best reasoning model clearly beats GPT-4o.
numbers: 3,400 test cases (GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench, Omni-MATH). Average F1: o1-mini 87.9, GPT-4o-0806 61.9; best open model QwQ-32B-Preview competitive with GPT-4o. Open critic models used majority vote over 8 samples; PRMs did poorly beyond GSM8K and MATH.
limits: Math only, first-error labelling, not hitting-set diagnosis. Table cells were garbled in text extraction; only figure-1 averages are quoted.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: error localisation in chains is feasible but weak for non-reasoning models; a QuickXplain-style bisection on chains has no direct test here.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (BIG-Bench Mistake)
finding: LLMs are poor at finding the mistake step in chain-of-thought traces, but good at fixing it when told where. A small trained classifier beat prompting a large model. Backtracking helps even with imperfect location.
numbers: GPT-4 best overall mistake-finding accuracy 52.87 with direct step-level prompting (5 tasks, 300 traces per task, 85% wrong traces). Tracking shuffled objects, GPT-4: 62.29 (direct trace), 65.33 (direct step), 90.67 (CoT step). Logical deduction GPT-4: 40.67/67.67/10.33. Backtracking losses plateau around 65% classifier accuracy.
limits: Older models (GPT-4, PaLM 2 Unicorn); CoT-step prompting raised mistake recall but cut accuracy on correct traces.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a noisy prefix-is-wrong oracle is exactly what QXR assumes. At about 65% accuracy, localise-then-fix still pays in this setting.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Verbalised confidence from LLMs is overconfident; values sit mostly at 80 to 100%. Prompting and sampling lower calibration error but failure prediction stays near chance.
numbers: 5 models, 8 tasks. GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna average ECE above 0.377. GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7% (random is 50%). White-box gap narrow: AUROC 0.522 vs 0.605. GPT-4 on GSM8K (93.6% accuracy) gets ECE 0.064 by saying 100%.
limits: Confidence on answers, not on which component is faulty. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: LLM-given fault probabilities are weak. Rodler (a19) found bad priors make random probing best, so default to uninformative priors.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: For RLHF models, verbalised confidence is better calibrated than token probabilities. Asking for several answer options with probabilities helps further.
numbers: ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude 2 on 3 QA datasets; verbalised prompts cut expected calibration error by over 50% relative to conditional probabilities.
limits: QA tasks. Calibration of a single answer, not a ranking of many suspects.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a useful but modest fix. Ask for a distribution over several suspects, expect only coarse calibration.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple choice and true/false when the format is right. P(True) self-evaluation improves when the model sees many of its own samples. P(IK) calibration fails on new tasks.
numbers: Anthropic models up to 52B parameters. A trained P(IK) probe generalises partly but calibration is weak out of distribution.
limits: Old models; probabilities about answer truth, not fault location.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: some signal exists for is-this-answer-right, which could stand in for a fault prior only after calibration on the same task type.

source: Bailis, Stoica, Zaharia, Zou (2024) Are More LM Calls All You Need?
finding: Vote and filter-vote systems can get better and then worse as the number of calls grows, because tasks mix easy and hard queries. The best call count can be predicted from a few samples.
numbers: Vote and Filter-Vote tested across several language tasks; peak then fall seen empirically. Scaling model predicts the optimal number of calls.
limits: Voting on single answers, not on conflict localisation.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: more calls is not free gain. Equal-call baselines need a tuned N, not the maximum.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Repeated sampling with an automatic verifier scales coverage log-linearly. Without verifiers, majority voting and reward models plateau.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 samples, versus single-sample state of the art 43%.
limits: Needs an exact verifier. QXR has only an LLM judge, the weak-verifier case.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the fair comparator for QXR is best-of-N at the same call budget. No paper has run it. Open.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: Accuracy depends on where the relevant item sits in the context: best at start or end, worst in the middle. Used here as a proxy for how a long suspect list is handled.
numbers: 20-document QA: GPT-3.5-Turbo closed-book 56.1%, oracle 88.3%; with the answer in the middle, accuracy fell below the closed-book 56.1%. MPT-30B-Instruct closed-book 31.5%, oracle 81.9%.
limits: QA retrieval, 2023 models. No test on suspect lists of different lengths.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: lists of 20 or more items already show position effects. A bounded frontier of 10-20 suspects is a design guess, not a measured threshold.
